'''''Juglans nigra''''', the '''eastern American black walnut''', is a species of [[deciduous]] tree in the [[walnut]] family, [[Juglandaceae]], native to central and eastern [[North America]], growing mostly in [[riparian zone]]s.

Black walnut is an important tree commercially, as the wood is a deep brown color and easily worked. Walnut [[seed]]s ([[nut (fruit)|nuts]]) are cultivated for their distinctive and desirable taste. Walnut trees are grown for lumber and food, and processors have found additional markets for even the tough outer hulls by finely grinding them for use in products such as abrasive cleansers. Many [[cultivar]]s have been developed for improved quality wood or nuts. In 2017, the [[United States Department of Agriculture]] valued U.S. walnut timber at $530 billion. A significant amount is grown in [[Missouri]].

Black walnut is [[allelopathic]], releasing chemicals from its roots and other tissues that may harm other organisms and give the tree a competitive advantage, but there is no [[scientific consensus]] that this is a primary competitive factor.

Black walnut is susceptible to [[thousand cankers disease]], which provoked a decline of walnut trees in some regions.

== Description ==
The tree grows to {{convert|30|-|40|m|ft|-1|abbr=on}} tall. Under forest competition, it develops a tall and straight [[Trunk (botany)|trunk]]. When grown in an open area it has a short trunk and broad crown.<ref name="dirr" /> The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is typically grey-black and deeply furrowed into thin ridges that gives the bark a diamond-shaped pattern.<ref name="dirr" />

The [[pith]] of the twigs is chambered and light brown.<ref name="peters">{{cite book|series=Peterson Field Guides|first1=George A. |last1=Petrides|title=A field guide to trees and shrubs: northeastern and north-central United States and southeastern and south-central Canada|date=1986|publisher=Houghton Mifflin|location=Boston|isbn=0-395-13651-2|edition=2nd|url=https://archive.org/details/fieldguidetotree00geor}}</ref> The [[bud]]s are pale silky and covered in downy hairs. The terminal buds are ovate, and {{convert|8|mm|in|frac=16|abbr=on}} long, and slightly longer than broad, the lateral buds are smaller and superposed.<ref name="dirr" />

The [[leaves]] are pinnately compound and alternately arranged on the stem. They are {{convert|30|–|60|cm|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long, typically [[even-pinnate]] but there is heavy variation among leaves. The stems have 15–23 leaflets, when terminal leaf is included, with the largest leaflets located in the center, {{convert|7|–|10|cm|frac=4|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2|–|3|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} broad.<ref name="dirr">{{cite book|last1=Dirr|first1=Michael A|title=Manual of woody landscape plants.|date=1990|publisher=Stipes Publishing Company|location=Champaign, Illinois|isbn=0-87563-344-7|edition=4. ed., rev.}}</ref> The leaflets have a rounded base and a long pointed ([[acuminate]]) tip as well as having a [[glossary of leaf morphology#serrated|serrated]] edge.<ref name="popa">{{cite book|title=The Plants of Pennsylvania|last2=Block|first2=Timothy|publisher=University of Pennsylvania press|isbn=978-0-8122-4003-0|edition=2nd|location=Philadelphia Pa|last1=Rhoads|first1=Ann|date=5 September 2007}}</ref> The leaves are overall dark green in color and are typically hairy on the underside.

The [[leaf scar]] has three prominent bundle scars<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Angier|first=Bradford|url=https://archive.org/details/fieldguidetoedib00angi/page/38/mode/2up|title=Field Guide to Edible Wild Plants|publisher=Stackpole Books|year=1974|isbn=0-8117-0616-8|location=Harrisburg, PA|page=38|oclc=799792|author-link=Bradford Angier}}</ref> and has a notch on the side that points toward the tip of the branch (distal side).

Black walnut is [[monoecious]]. The male ([[staminate]]) flowers are in drooping [[catkins]] {{convert|8|–|10|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} long. These are borne from axillary buds on the previous year's growth. The female ([[pistillate]]) flowers are terminal, in clusters of two to five on the current year's growth.<ref name="Silvics">{{Silvics|volume=2|genus=Juglans|species=nigra|first=Robert D.|last=Williams|access-date=2016-06-29}}</ref> During the summer/autumn, a spherical fruit (nut) ripens. It comprises a brownish-green, semifleshy husk and a brown, corrugated nut. The whole fruit, including the husk, falls in October; the seed is relatively small and very hard.

Most parts of the tree including leaves, stems, and fruit [[husk]]s have a very characteristic pungent or spicy odor. This odor is lacking in the nut itself.<ref name="dirr" /><ref name="peters" />

=== Similar species ===
[[Juglans cinerea|''J. cinerea'']] (the butternut) is similar in leaf shape and range. The fruits are quite different, as black walnut fruits are spherical and butternuts are more oval-oblong. When a fruit is not available, two species can be differentiated based on the leaf scars: the butternut's has a flat upper edge and with a velvety ridge above that flat part, but black walnut's is indented with no hairy ridge.<ref>{{eFloras|1|116860|Juglans |family=Juglandaceae |first1=Alan T. |last1=Whittemore |first2=Donald E. |last2=Stone}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
The species is native to [[North America]]. It grows mostly in [[riparian zone]]s, from southern [[Ontario]], west to southeast [[South Dakota]], south to [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], northern [[Florida]] and southwest to central [[Texas]]. Wild trees in the upper [[Ottawa Valley]] may be an isolated native population or may have derived from planted trees. The range of the black walnut is strongly correlated with low maximum [[vapour-pressure deficit]].<ref>{{cite journal |date=2024-10-18 |first1=Narayani |last1=Barve |first2=Uzma |last2=Ashraf |first3=Vijay |last3=Barve |first4=Marlon E. |last4=Cobos |first5=Claudia |last5=Nuñez-Penichet |first6=Andrew |last6=Townsend Peterson |title=Revisiting plant hardiness zones to include multiple climatic stress dimensions |article-number=110824 |doi=10.1016/j.isci.2024.110824 |journal=iScience |eissn=2589-0042 |volume=27 |issue=10|pmid=39435139 |pmc=11491728 |bibcode=2024iSci...27k0824B }}</ref>

== Ecology ==
Black walnut is primarily a [[pioneer species]] similar to [[red maple|red]] and [[silver maple]] and [[black cherry]]. Because of this, black walnut is a common weed tree found along roadsides, fields, and forest edges in the eastern US. It will grow in closed forests, but is classified as shade intolerant; this means it requires full sun for optimal growth and nut production.

Black walnut's native range extends across much of the eastern US. It is absent from the coastal plain south of [[North Carolina]] as well as the Mississippi Valley, and does not occur in the northern tier of the eastern US, where the frost-free season is too short for the nuts to develop. Its western range extends all the way to the eastern Great Plains, beyond which climate conditions become too dry for it.

Black walnut is one of the most abundant trees in the eastern US, particularly the Northeast, and its numbers are increasing due to epidemics that have affected other tree species, including emerald ash borer, chestnut blight, butternut canker, wooly hemlock adelgid, dogwood anthracnose, Dutch elm disease, and spongy moth infestations. Widespread clear-cutting of oaks due to spongy moth damage in the 1970s–1980s particularly aided in the tree's spread. The aggressive competitive strategy of black walnut such as its fast growth, alleopathic chemicals, and rodent-dispersed seeds, have also contributed.
[[File:Black walnut fruits on the ground.jpg|thumb|190px|Walnuts fallen from a tree]]

The nuts are food for many rodents and make up to 10% of the diet of [[eastern fox squirrel]]s.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="FEIS">{{FEIS |type=tree |genus=Juglans |species=nigra |last=Coladonato |first=Milo |date=1991 |access-date=2016-06-29}}</ref> The nuts are also eaten by species of birds. The leaves are browsed by [[white tailed deer]],<ref name="FEIS" /> although they are not a preferred food.

Where the range of the eastern black walnut overlaps that of the Texas black walnut (''[[Juglans microcarpa|J. microcarpa]]''), the two species sometimes interbreed, producing populations with characteristics intermediate between the two species.<ref>{{FEIS |type=tree |genus=Juglans |species=microcarpa |last=Tirmenstein |first=D. A. |date=1990 |access-date=2016-06-29}}</ref> ''J. nigra'' and ''J. cinerea'' often grow in the same range as well but they do not hybridize naturally.<ref name="Silvics" /><ref name="FEIS" />

The tree's roots often form [[endomycorrhiza]]l relationships with fungi in the genus [[Glomus (fungus)|''Glomus'']]. Some endomycorrhizal relations improve the plant's growth.<ref name="Silvics" />

Species often associated with ''J. nigra'' include [[yellow-poplar]] (''Liriodendron tulipifera''), [[Fraxinus americana|white ash]] (''Fraxinus americana''), [[black cherry]] (''Prunus serotina''), [[basswood]] (''Tilia americana''), [[American beech]] (''Fagus grandifolia''), [[sugar maple]] (''Acer saccharum''), [[oak]]s (''Quercus'' spp.), and [[hickory|hickories]] (''Carya'' spp.). Near the western edge of its range, black walnut may be confined to floodplains, where it grows either with [[American elm]] (''Ulmus americana''), [[common hackberry]] (''Celtis occidentalis''), [[green ash]] (''Fraxinus pennsylvanica''), and [[boxelder]] (''Acer negundo''), or with basswood and [[red oak]] (''Quercus rubra'') on lower slopes and other favorable sites.<ref name="Silvics" />

=== Pests ===
[[Maggot]]s (larvae of ''[[Rhagoletis completa]]'' and ''[[Rhagoletis suavis]]'') in the husk are common, though more a nuisance than a serious problem for amateurs, who may simply remove the affected husk as soon as infestation is noticed. The maggots develop entirely within the husk, thus the quality of the nutmeat is not affected.<ref>{{cite report | last1=Weber | first1=Barbara C. | last2=Anderson | first2=Robert L. | last3=Hoffard | first3=William H. | title=How to diagnose black walnut damage. | publisher=U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, North Central Forest Experiment Station | publication-place=St. Paul, MN | year=1980 | doi=10.2737/nc-gtr-57 | doi-access=free | url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/pubs/download/10122.pdf | page=13 | chapter=Walnut Husk Fly and Husk Maggot}}{{dead link|date=June 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>  However, infestations of maggots are undesirable because they make the husk difficult to remove and are unsightly.  Maggots can be serious for commercial walnut growers, who tend to use chemical treatments to prevent damage to the crop.<ref>{{cite web | title=Walnut Husk Maggot | website=Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs | date=2006-12-19 | url=http://www.omafra.gov.on.ca/english/crops/hort/news/hortmatt/2004/28hrt04a8.htm | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081011111952/http://www.omafra.gov.on.ca/english/crops/hort/news/hortmatt/2004/28hrt04a8.htm | archive-date=2008-10-11 }}</ref>  Some non-chemical controls also exist, such as removing and disposing of infested nuts.<ref>{{cite web |title=Walnut Husk Fly Management Guidelines – UC IPM |url=http://www.ipm.ucdavis.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7430.html |website=www.ipm.ucdavis.edu}}</ref>

The walnut [[weevil]] (''[[Conotrachelus retentus]]'') grows to {{convert|5|mm|in|frac=16}} long as an adult. The adult sucks plant juices through a snout.  The eggs are laid in fruits in the spring and summer. Many nuts are lost due to damage from the larvae, which burrow through the nut shell.<ref>{{cite web |title=Northeastern Area State and Private Forestry |url=http://na.fs.fed.us/spfo/pubs/howtos/ht_walnut/curculio.htm |website=na.fs.fed.us}}</ref>

Black walnut is affected by European canker (''[[Neonectria galligena]]''). The infection spreads slowly but infected trees eventually die.<ref name="FEIS" />

[[File:Black walnut caterpillars.jpg|thumb|Walnut caterpillars]] The walnut caterpillar (''[[Datana integerrima]]'') and fall webworm (''[[Hyphantria cunea]]'') are two of the most serious pests, they commonly eat the foliage in midsummer and continue into autumn.

Codling moth (''[[Cydia pomonella]]'') larvae eat walnut kernels, as well as apple and pear seeds.<ref>{{cite web |title=Codling Moth Management Guidelines – UC IPM |url=http://www.ipm.ucdavis.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7412.html |website=www.ipm.ucdavis.edu}}</ref>

Important leaf sucking insects include species of [[aphid]]s and plant lice including (''[[Monellia]]'' spp. and ''[[Monelliopsis]]'' spp.), which suck the juices from leaves and often deposit a sticky substance called "honey-dew" on the leaf surface that may turn black and prevent photosynthesis; and the walnut lace bug (''[[Corythucha juglandis]]''), which causes damage when the adults and nymphs suck the sap from the lower surfaces of walnut leaflets.<ref name="Silvics" />

A disease complex known as [[thousand cankers disease]] has been threatening black walnut in several western states.<ref>{{cite web |title=Pest Alert: Walnut Twig Beetle and Thousand Cankers Disease of Black Walnut |url=http://www.ppdl.purdue.edu/PPDL/pubs/walnutthousandcankersdisease.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100628184055/http://www.ppdl.purdue.edu/PPDL/pubs/walnutthousandcankersdisease.pdf |archive-date=2010-06-28 |access-date=2010-08-06 |publisher=Purdue University: Purdue Pest & Plant Diagnostic Laboratory}}</ref>  This disease has recently been discovered in Tennessee, and could potentially have devastating effects on the species in the eastern United States.<ref>{{cite web |title=Bill Poovey. Black walnut tree thousand canker first in East US. ''Times Union''. Posted July 30, 2010. |url=http://www.timesunion.com/news/article/Black-walnut-tree-thousand-canker-first-in-East-US-597229.php}}</ref> Vectored by the walnut twig beetle (''[[Pityophthorus juglandis]]''), a fungus, ''[[Geosmithia morbida]]'', spreads into the wood around the galleries carved by the small beetles.  The fungus causes cankers that inhibit the movement of nutrients in black walnut, leading to crown and branch dieback, and ultimately death.<ref>{{cite web |title=Walnut Twig Beetle, Thousand Cankers Disease |url=http://www.clemson.edu/public/regulatory/plant_industry/pest_nursery_programs/invasive_exotic_programs/pest_alerts/walnut_twig_beetle.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141213005045/http://www.clemson.edu/public/regulatory/plant_industry/pest_nursery_programs/invasive_exotic_programs/pest_alerts/walnut_twig_beetle.html |archive-date=13 December 2014 |publisher=Clemson University |location=South Carolina}}</ref>

=== Allelopathy ===
While black walnut is considered [[allelopathic]], meaning it excretes chemicals into its environment that harm competition, research from 2019 has questioned whether this long-held belief holds up to scientifically rigorous examination. Many publications that have repeated claims of black walnut allelopathy cite a very limited set of dated research literature, which has not held up to scientific scrutiny.<ref name=":1">{{Cite report |url=http://hdl.handle.net/2376/14212 |title=Do black walnut trees have allelopathic effects on other plants? |last=Chalker-Scott |first=Linda |access-date=2022-09-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220919123846/https://rex.libraries.wsu.edu/esploro/outputs/report/Do-black-walnut-trees-have-allelopathic/99900501686101842 |archive-date=19 September 2022 |url-status=live |website=rex.libraries.wsu.edu |hdl=2376/14212 |number=FS325E |series=Home Garden Series}}</ref> Anecdotally, records of walnut toxicity to other plants have been observed as far back as the first century when [[Pliny the Elder]] wrote: "The shadow of walnut trees is poison to all plants within its compass."<ref name="cheme">{{cite journal |last1=Rietvelt |first1=W. J |date=1983 |title=Allelopathic effects of juglone on germination and growth of several herbaceous and woody species |url=http://www.nrs.fs.fed.us/pubs/jrnl/1983/nc_1983_rietveld_001.pdf |journal=Journal of Chemical Ecology |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=295–308 |bibcode=1983JCEco...9..295R |doi=10.1007/BF00988047 |pmid=24407348 |s2cid=23491349 |access-date=2 July 2016}}</ref> 

Like other walnuts, the roots, inner bark, nut husks, and leaves contain a nontoxic chemical called hydrojuglone;<ref name="cheme" /> when exposed to air or soil compounds it is oxidized into [[juglone]] that is biologically active and acts as a respiratory inhibitor to some plants. Juglone is poorly soluble in water and does not move far in the soil and will stay most concentrated in the soil directly beneath the tree.<ref name="per">{{cite web |title=Black walnut toxicity |url=https://www.hort.purdue.edu/ext/HO-193.pdf |access-date=30 June 2016 |publisher=Purdue University}}</ref> Even after a tree is removed the soil where the roots once were will still contain juglone for several years after the tree is removed as more juglone will be released as the roots decay.<ref name="per" /> Well drained and aerated soils will host a healthy community of soil microbes and these microbes will help to break down the juglone.

Symptoms of juglone poisoning include foliar yellowing and wilting.<ref name="per" /> A number of plants are particularly sensitive.  Apples, tomatoes, pines, and birch are poisoned by juglone, and as a precaution, should not be planted in proximity to a black walnut.<ref name="Silvics" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Black Walnut Toxicity |url=http://www.wvu.edu/~agexten/hortcult/fruits/blkwalnt.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150212041801/http://www.wvu.edu/~agexten/hortcult/fruits/blkwalnt.htm |archive-date=12 February 2015 |access-date=3 July 2014 |publisher=West Virginia University}}</ref>

=== Interaction with horses ===
Horses are susceptible to [[laminitis]] from exposure to black walnut wood in bedding.<ref>{{cite web |date=January 2005 |title=Laminitis Caused by Black Walnut Wood Residues |url=http://www.ces.purdue.edu/extmedia/FNR/FNR-254.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100614205517/http://www.ces.purdue.edu/extmedia/FNR/FNR-254.pdf |archive-date=14 June 2010 |access-date=9 March 2009 |publisher=Purdue University}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Black walnut tree.jpg|thumb|A young black walnut tree full of fruit in [[Eastern Oklahoma]]]] The fruit production tends to occur irregularly with some years producing larger crops than others (see [[mast year]]). Fruiting may begin when the tree is 4–6 years old, but large crops take 20 years. Total lifespan of ''J. nigra'' is about 130 years. Like other trees of the order [[Fagales]], such as oaks, hickories, chestnuts, and birches, it is monoecious, with wind-pollinated catkins. Male and female flowers are in separate [[spike (botany)|spikes]], and the female flowers typically appear before the male on a single tree ([[dichogamy]]). As a consequence, [[self-pollination]] is unlikely. However, individual trees are commonly self-compatible; if they are not pollinated by neighboring trees, they may set self-fertilized seeds.<ref name="Silvics" /> For maximum seed germination, the seeds should be [[cold-moist stratified]] for 3–4 months, although the exact time depends on the seed source.<ref name="Silvics" /> The seedlings emerge in April or May. While most trees with taproots have a reputation for slow growth, black walnut is an exception and can achieve very rapid growth in the seedling stage, typically {{convert|90|cm|in|round=5|abbr=on}} their first year and even more in the second year.<ref name="Silvics" /> Black walnut will not leaf out until temperatures have warmed sufficiently. Leafout in spring is initiated when daytime highs reach approximately {{cvt|70|°F}} and leaf drop in fall when daytime highs fall below {{cvt|65|°F|°C}}. As such, the exact timing will vary in different regions of the U.S. and depending on the weather conditions from year to year, leafout is typically early April in the southern part of its range and sometimes not until the end of May or beginning of June in cooler areas. Leaf drop in fall may begin in late September in cooler regions and not until November in southern areas.<ref name="Silvics" />

Black walnut is more resistant to frost than ''[[Juglans regia|J. regia]]'' (the English or Persian walnut), but thrives best in the warmer regions of fertile, lowland soils with high water tables, although it will also grow in drier soils, but much more slowly.<ref name="dirr" /> Some specimens have been found to survive frosts down to {{cvt|−45|°F}}.<ref name="Silvics" /> Some soils preferred by black walnut include [[alfisol]] and [[entisol]] soil types.<ref name="Silvics" /> Black walnut grows best on sandy loam, loam, or silt loam type soils but will also grow well on silty clay loam soils. It prefers these soils because they hold large quantities of water, which the tree draws from during rainless periods.<ref name="Silvics" />
=== Planting ===
Black walnut has a strong [[taproot]], which makes the seedlings resilient, but difficult to transplant.[[File:Black walnut cracked open to expose meat.jpg|thumb|Seed shell cracked open to expose kernel. Under the right conditions, a black walnut tree will sprout and grow from a seed like the one pictured here.<ref>{{cite web |title=How can I germinate walnuts? |url=https://hortnews.extension.iastate.edu/faq/how-can-i-germinate-walnuts |website=[[Iowa State University]] |access-date=3 December 2022}}</ref>]] While its primary native region is the Midwest and east-central United States, the black walnut was introduced into Europe, likely in the year 1629, where it has gained economic significance.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nicolescu |first1=Valeriu-Norocel |last2=Rédei |first2=Károly |last3=Vor |first3=Torsten |last4=Bastien |first4=Jean-Charles |last5=Brus |first5=Robert |last6=Benčať |first6=Tibor |last7=Đodan |first7=Martina |last8=Cvjetkovic |first8=Branislav |last9=Andrašev |first9=Siniša |last10=La Porta |first10=Nicola |last11=Lavnyy |first11=Vasyl |last12=Petkova |first12=Krasimira |last13=Perić |first13=Sanja |last14=Bartlett |first14=Debbie |last15=Hernea |first15=Cornelia |date=2020-10-01 |title=A review of black walnut (Juglans nigra L.) ecology and management in Europe | doi-access=free | url=https://zenodo.org/records/4264908/files/2020%20Nicolescu_et_al%20-%20Black_walnut_Trees_2020_final.pdf |journal=Trees |language=en |volume=34 |issue=5 |pages=1087–1112 |doi=10.1007/s00468-020-01988-7 |bibcode=2020Trees..34.1087N |issn=1432-2285}}</ref> It is also cultivated in Hawaii.<ref name="FEIS" /> It is cultivated as a forest tree for its high-quality wood. Black walnut plantings can be made to produce timber, nuts, or both timber and nuts. Patented timber-type trees were selected and released from [[Purdue University]] in the early 1990s. These trees have been sporadically available from [[Plant nursery|nurseries]]. Varieties include Purdue #1, which can be used for both timber and nut production, though nut quality is poor compared to varieties selected specifically as nut producers.

[[File:2014-10-30 10 16 45 Black Walnut foliage during autumn along Fireside Avenue in Ewing, New Jersey.JPG|thumb|Autumn foliage]]

[[Grafted]], nut-producing trees are available from several nurseries operating in the U.S. Selections worth considering include Thomas, Neel #1, Thomas Myers, Pounds #2, Stoker, Surprise, Emma K, Sparrow, S127, and McGinnis. Several older varieties, such as Kwik Krop, are still in cultivation; while they make decent nuts, they would not be recommended for commercial planting.<ref name="MU-Extension">{{cite web | title=Flowering and Fruit Characteristics of Black Walnuts: A Tool for Identifying and Selecting Cultivars | website=[[University of Missouri Extension]] | url=http://extension.missouri.edu/publications/xm1001?p=1 | access-date=2021-10-29}}</ref>

Pollination requirements should be considered when planting black walnuts. As is typical of many species in Juglandaceae, ''J. nigra'' trees tend to be monoecious, i.e.. produce [[pollen]] first and then [[Gynoecium#Pistil|pistillate flowers]] or else produce pistillate flowers and then pollen. An early pollen-producer should be grouped with other varieties that produce pistillate flowers so all varieties benefit from overlap. Cranz, Thomas, and Neel #1 make a good pollination trio. A similar group for more northern climates would be Sparrow, S127, and Mintle.

Sometimes black walnut is planted as part of reclaiming mines.<ref name="FEIS" /> When growing young trees weed control is critical for healthy establishment of the trees, without weed control the young trees are harmed significantly in their growth rate.

===Commercial===
[[File:Black Walnuts (Juglans nigra) hulled and shelled, meat only.jpg|thumb|A bowl of black walnut kernels, shelled]]

Black walnuts are shelled commercially in the United States. With about 65% of the U.S.'s annual wild harvest,<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 26, 2019 |title=Nuts of Missouri {{!}} Missouri's Natural Heritage {{!}} Washington University in St. Louis |url=https://sites.wustl.edu/monh/nuts-of-missouri/ |access-date=2024-09-24 |website=sites.wustl.edu}}</ref> the U.S. state of [[Missouri]] is home to the world's largest processor and distributor of black walnuts, which the [[Missouri Department of Conservation]] considers to be the state's most valuable timber.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Hilgedick |first=Kristie |date=October 1, 2017 |title=Bountiful, Beneficial Black Walnuts |url=https://mdc.mo.gov/magazines/conservationist/2017-10/bountiful-beneficial-black-walnuts |access-date=2024-09-24 |website=Missouri Department of Conservation |language=en}}</ref> In 1990, Missouri named the "Eastern Black Walnut" as its official tree nut.<ref>{{Cite web |title=RSMo § 10.100 |url=https://www.revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=10.100&bid=329 |access-date=2024-09-24 |website=revisor.mo.gov |language=en}}</ref> Missouri's largest processing plant is operated by Hammons Products in [[Stockton, Missouri]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Association |first=Missouri Nut Growers |title=Missouri Nut Growers Association |url=https://missourinutgrowers.org/walnuts |access-date=2024-09-24 |website=Missouri Nut Growers Association |language=en-US}}</ref> [[NPR]] affiliate [[KCUR]] stated in an article that "Ralph Hammons began the company in 1946 with a nut cracking machine acquired from Tennessee."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Bailey, Hogan |first1=Natasha, Suzanne |title=Black walnuts don't get as much love as non-native nuts. These Missourians want to change that |url=https://www.kcur.org/arts-life/2022-12-07/black-walnuts-missouri-stockton-hammons-beer-nuts |access-date=8 December 2022 |agency=[[KCUR]] |publisher=[[NPR]] |date=December 7, 2022}}</ref> The Stockton ''Black Walnut Festival'', which has been held annually since 1961, "brings the community together for a 3-day event jam-packed with activities including a carnival, tractor pull, nut roll and 2-hour parade," stated Alexa Hodges in a [[Columbia Missourian|VOX]] article.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hodges |first1=Alexa |title=What you should know before you go to the Black Walnut Festival |url=https://www.voxmagazine.com/food/what-you-should-know-before-you-go-to-the-black-walnut-festival/article_e93199e6-c078-11e8-a468-538e1051ea42.html |access-date=8 December 2022 |agency=[[Columbia Missourian|VOX]] |date=September 28, 2018}}</ref>

====Nut processing by hand====
[[File:Hands after hulling 500 black walnuts.jpg|thumb|Hand stains after removing the husks from black walnuts]]
[[File:Juglans nigra vs. Juglans regia – shell comparison.jpg|thumb|The black walnut (left) is harder to process than the [[English walnut]] (right)]]

The extraction of the kernel from the fruit of the black walnut is difficult.  The thick, hard shell is tightly bound by tall ridges to a thick husk. Rolling the nut underfoot on a hard surface such as a driveway is a common method; commercial huskers use a car tire rotating against a metal mesh.  Some take a thick plywood board and drill a nut-sized hole in it (from one to two inches in diameter) and smash the nut through using a hammer. The nut goes through and the husk remains behind.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://web.extension.illinois.edu/cfiv/homeowners/991002.html|author=Mason, Sandra|title=Preparing Black Walnuts for Eating|publisher=University of Illinois Extension|access-date=2014-07-26|archive-date=2014-07-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140730034154/http://web.extension.illinois.edu/cfiv/homeowners/991002.html}}</ref> American pioneers let the nuts dry in the sun, then removed the husks and let the kernels dry—making them less bitter.<ref name=":0" />

The shell itself is thicker than that of the English walnut, and there are additional, thick internal walls tightly surrounding the nutmeat. Walnuts are too tough and too large to be opened with a standard nutcracker, but simply cracking the shell open with a rock results in smashed and shattered nutmeats mixed with shell, unless done with some care and skill—and it is still nearly impossible to extract an intact half this way. As a result, a number of home walnut-cracking devices have been produced, involving vices, cams, or levers.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://johnsankey.ca/nutcracker.html|author=John Sankey|title=Black Walnut Crackers|access-date=2020-11-24}}</ref>

While the flavor of the ''Juglans nigra'' kernel is prized, the difficulty in preparing it may account for the wider popularity and availability of the English walnut.

===Ornamental===
''J. nigra'' is also grown as a specimen ornamental tree in parks and large gardens, growing to {{cvt|30|m|ft|round=5}} tall by {{cvt|20|m|ft||round=5}} broad.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1-4053-3296-5|page=1136}}</ref> It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=''Juglans nigra''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/9503/Juglans-nigra-(F)/Details|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=25 September 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 56 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 14 March 2018 | archive-date = 5 January 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180105180412/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | url-status = live }}</ref>

===As food===

Black walnut kernels are edible.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Lyle|first=Katie Letcher|title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants, Mushrooms, Fruits, and Nuts: How to Find, Identify, and Cook Them|publisher=[[FalconGuides]]|year=2010|isbn=978-1-59921-887-8|edition=2nd|location=Guilford, CN|page=134|oclc=560560606|orig-date=2004}}</ref> The nut provides a robust, distinctive, natural flavor and crunch as a food ingredient. Common uses include ice cream, bakery goods and confections.  Consumers include black walnuts in traditional treats, such as [[cake]]s, [[cookie]]s, [[fudge]], and [[pie]]s, during the fall holiday season.  The nuts are versatile for uses in other foods, such as [[salad]]s, [[fish]], [[pork]], [[chicken]], vegetables and pasta dishes.

Tapped in spring, the tree yields a sweet sap that can be drunk or concentrated into syrup or sugar not unlike that of [[sugar maple]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://smallfarms.cornell.edu/2016/01/11/tapping-walnut-trees/|title=Tapping Walnut Trees for a Novel and Delicious Syrup|date=2016-01-11|website=Cornell Small Farms Program|access-date=2019-02-01}}</ref>

====Nutrition====
Black walnut kernels are 5% water, 59% [[fat]], 24% [[protein (nutrient)|protein]], and 10% [[carbohydrate]]s. In a reference amount of {{cvt|100|g}}, walnuts supply 619 [[calorie]]s and several [[micronutrient]]s in rich amounts at 20% or more of the [[Daily Value]] (DV), including the [[mineral (nutrient)|dietary minerals]] [[manganese in biology|manganese]] (169% DV) and [[copper in biology|copper]] (156% DV), among others, and the [[B vitamins]], [[vitamin B6|B<sub>6</sub>]] (34% DV) and [[pantothenic acid]] (33% DV). Black walnut kernels are a moderate source (10–19% DV) of [[vitamin E]] and [[riboflavin]].<ref name=nutrition>Source in table</ref>

Analysis of black walnut fat content showed the most prevalent [[fatty acid]]s are [[linoleic acid]] (33.8%), followed by [[oleic acid]] (15.3%), [[alpha-linolenic acid]] (2.7%), [[palmitic acid]] (1.9%), and [[stearic acid]] (1.5%).<ref name=nutrition/>

=== Dye ===
Black walnut [[drupe]]s contain juglone (5-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone), [[plumbagin]] (yellow quinone pigments), and [[tannin]]. These compounds cause walnuts to stain cars, sidewalks, porches, and patios, in addition to the hands of anyone attempting to shell them.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.drugs.com/npp/black-walnut.html|title=Black Walnut Uses, Benefits & Dosage – Drugs.com Herbal Database|access-date=2018-01-23|archive-date=2018-07-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180704092837/https://www.drugs.com/npp/black-walnut.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The brownish-black dye was used by early American settlers to dye hair.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.faculty.ucr.edu/~legneref/botany/legunuts.htm|title=Legumes, Nuts, Seeds & discussion|website=www.faculty.ucr.edu}}</ref>{{Better source needed|reason=Source is marked ''For teaching purposes only; do not review, quote or abstract''|date=July 2014}} According to Eastern Trees in the Petersen Guide series, black walnuts make a yellowish-brown dye, not brownish-black. The apparent confusion is easily explained by the fact that the liquid (dye) obtained from the inner husk becomes increasingly darker over time, as the outer skin darkens from light green to black. Extracts of the outer, soft part of the drupe are still used as a [[natural dye]] for handicrafts.<ref>{{cite web | title=Black Walnut Dye Recipes and Supplies | website=basketmakers.org | date=2008-08-07 | url=http://basketmakers.org/topics/tutorials/walnutdye.htm | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081010184908/http://basketmakers.org/topics/tutorials/walnutdye.htm | archive-date=2008-10-10 | url-status=usurped }}</ref> The tannins present in walnuts act as a [[mordant]], aiding in the dyeing process,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pburch.net/dyeing/dyelog/B1063361308/C1605100905/E20061005114406/|title=Fixing natural dyes from walnuts, goldenrod, sassafras and poke weed in cotton – do I use urea or soda ash?|website=www.pburch.net}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bayrose.org/Poppy_Run/dyeing2_web.pdf|title=Dyeing with Tannic Acid and Iron: Walnut Husks (2005)}}</ref> and are usable as a dark ink or wood stain.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://home.insightbb.com/~denevell_books/making_walnut_ink.htm |title=Making Walnut Ink |author=Madame Elizabeth de Nevell}}</ref>

=== Shells ===
Walnut shells are often used as an abrasive in sand blasting or other circumstances where a medium hardness grit is required. The hard black walnut shell is also used commercially in abrasive cleaning, a filtering agent in scrubbers in smoke stacks, cleaning jet engines, cosmetics, and oil well drilling and water filtration.<ref name="FEIS" /> Additionally, the husks are ground into an ingredient in exfoliating cosmetics.<ref name=":2" />

=== Wood ===
[[File:S1, S2, S3 (3542257521).jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Black walnut wood showing the color and grain]]
[[File:Juglans nigra MHNT.BOT.2018.6.22.jpg|thumb|Wood in cross section]]

Black walnut is highly prized for its dark-colored, straight grained, true heartwood. It is heavy, strong, shock resistant and yet can be easily split and worked. Along with cedars ([[Thuja|''Thuja spp.'']]), chestnut ([[Castanea (genus)|''Castanea spp'']].), and black locust (''[[Robinia pseudoacacia]]'') black walnut is one of the most durable hardwoods in the US.<ref name="FEIS" /> The wood can be kiln dried and holds its shape well after seasoning, which makes this wood even more attractive for wood working.<ref name="FEIS" />

Walnut wood has historically been used for [[gun stock]]s, furniture, flooring, paddles, coffins, and a variety of other wood products.<ref name="FEIS" /> Black walnut has a density of 660 kg per cubic meter (41.2 lb/cubic foot),<ref>{{cite web | title=Black Walnut | website=nichetimbers.co.uk | date=2008-10-21 | url=http://www.nichetimbers.co.uk/hardwood/north-american-hardwood/black-walnut/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080811233253/http://www.nichetimbers.co.uk/hardwood/north-american-hardwood/black-walnut/ | archive-date=2008-08-11 }}</ref> which makes it less dense than oak.

== Largest trees ==
The [[National Register of Champion Trees|U.S. national champion]] black walnut, also known locally as the Sauvie Island Tree<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fallen But Not Forgotten - The Legacy of Sauvie Island's Giant Walnut |url=https://gobywalnut.com/blogs/articles/nations-largest-black-walnut-tree-national-champion |access-date=2026-08-08 |website=Goby Walnut Products, Inc}}</ref>, was situated on a residential property on [[Sauvie Island]], [[Oregon]]. It was {{convert|8|ft|7|in|m|abbr=on}} [[diameter at breast height]] and {{convert|112|ft|abbr=on}} tall, with a crown spread of {{convert|144|ft}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ascendingthegiants.com/oregon-big-tree-registry.html|title=Oregon Champion Tree Registry|date=2013|website=ascendingthegiants.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160308132251/http://ascendingthegiants.com/oregon-big-tree-registry.html|archive-date=2016-03-08}}</ref>

In the mid-2010s, it was clear that the tree was in [[Plant disease|visible decline]]. In 2019, it was confirmed that the tree was succumbing to [[Thousand cankers disease|Thousand Cankers Disease]], and plans were set in place to fell the tree to mitigate the risk of [[Plant disease forecasting|disease being spread]].

In August 2020, [[Arborist|workers]] brought down the tree with the use of specialised equipment. 

Slabs cut from the tree have been salvaged for reuse, as the timber is highly regarded in the [[woodworking]] industry.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fallen But Not Forgotten - The Legacy of Sauvie Island's Giant Walnut |url=https://gobywalnut.com/blogs/articles/nations-largest-black-walnut-tree-national-champion |access-date=2026-08-08 |website=Goby Walnut Products, Inc}}</ref> 

[[File:Sauvie Island Black Walnut.jpg|thumb|Sauvie Island Tree, once the largest known black walnut tree in North America on [[Sauvie Island]], Oregon, before it was felled in August 2020 due to [[Thousand cankers disease|Thousand Cankers Disease]].]]

The tallest black walnut in Europe is located in the Woluwe Park in the city of Sint-Pieters-Woluwe, Brussels, Belgium. It has a circumference of {{convert|3.50|m|ftin|abbr=on}}, height of exactly {{convert|33.60|m|ft|abbr=on}} (measured by laser), and was planted around 1850 (± 10 years).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.monumentaltrees.com/nl/bel/brussel/sintpieterswoluwe/85_parkvanwoluwe/4031/|title=Zwarte walnoot in het park van Woluwe, Sint-Pieters-Woluwe, Brussel, België}}</ref>

The largest black walnut in Europe is located in the Castle Park in the city of [[Sereď]], Slovakia. It has a circumference of {{convert|6.30|m|ftin|abbr=on}}, height of {{convert|25|m|ft|abbr=on}} and estimated age of 300 years.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.seredonline.sk/clanky/mesto-sered-ma-unikatny-strom-juglans-nigra-nominovany-v-sutazi-strom-roka-2012/|title=Mesto Sereď má unikátny strom Juglans nigra nominovaný v súťaži Strom roka 2012 - SereďOnLine|first=Majko Design Studio - Miloš|last=Majko|access-date=2012-06-18|archive-date=2012-10-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121020212214/http://www.seredonline.sk/clanky/mesto-sered-ma-unikatny-strom-juglans-nigra-nominovany-v-sutazi-strom-roka-2012/}}</ref>
